item.title: AI selloff rejuvenates Asia's forgotten investment trades
item.description: Retreat from AI-linked stocks prompts investors to look towards undervalued markets such as India and China, while easing inflation and trade tensions add to their appeal ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: The unravelling of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade after the US midterm elections is forcing investors to rethink their Asiaplaybook, reviving demand for out-of-favour Chinese and Indian stocks, and companies poised to benefit from easinginflation and trade tensions. Aberdeen Investments favours markets powered by stronger domestic growth, including India and Vietnam, and sees upside in Chinese technology firms.  Asia has been among the hardest hit by the market fallout from the Democrats’ sweep of US Congress. Many of the region’s biggest stocks are critical suppliers to the global AI buildout, leaving local markets exposed as investors brace forgreater scrutiny of the industry. “I expect investors to diversify more broadly and reduce their concentration in the AI trade,” said Rajeev De Mello, global macro portfolio manager at Gama Asset Management SA. “This should be supportive of China and other markets where valuations areless demanding,” he said. India’s appeal has grown as oil prices fell on expectations of an earlier end to the Iran war. Its lack of AI exposure is also now seen as an advantage. LOGOS Asset Management’s Charlie Hong said he sold his shares in SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Intel and Lumentum Holdings last month and has since boosted his Indian holdings. India’s benchmark Nifty 50 gained 8.6 per cent last week, registering its best week since 2021, as overseas investors returned in force.

item.title: EU close to deal to link UK carbon market nearly six years after Brexit
item.description: The agreement, to be announced at a key summit later this month, would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Ewa Krukowska and John Ainger The European Union and the UK are in the final stages of a deal to link their emissions markets, a move that would boost liquidity and eventually save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes. The agreement, to be announced at a key summit later this month, would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems, almost six years after Britain started its own cap-and-trade program in the wake of Brexit. Negotiators have already ironed out details on emissions caps, supply controls and free permits, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The treatment of financial derivatives is the only outstanding issue.  The EU’s carbon market is the region’s key way to meet its carbon reduction goals. Started in 2005, the market imposes gradually shrinking emissions limits on around 10,000 facilities in sectors from steel and cement to fertilizers, power production and aviation. Once linked, it will allow mutual recognition of permits from both markets for compliance, helpful for companies with operations in both regions. The linkage deal is set to be one of the main deliverables at the Nov. 20 meeting of UK and EU leaders, alongside matching university tuition fees for students traveling between the two. Other areas of agreement include committing to minimizing the effect of their trade measures on vulnerable sectors like steel and electric cars, and deepening cooperation on cyber threats, Bloomberg reported last month. The European Commission declined to comment on the agreement, in line with its long-standing policy of not commenting on draft documents.  The agreement will not automatically exempt the parties from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms, which put emissions costs on certain imported products to shield local producers against competitors from regions with laxer climate rules. Instead, it will pave the way for a waiver once the parties fulfill certain condition embedded in their domestic laws, the people said. The EU law sets two requirements for such a move: full linkage with its ETS and effective carbon pricing without preferential rebates. Once those are met, the EU will add the UK to a list of countries outside of the CBAM regulation scope via a delegated act.  While the EU carbon border tax became operational this year, with the first compliance deadline set for September, the UK mechanism is to kick off at the start of 2027.  UK carbon prices have already narrowed their discount to the EU ETS market since the two parties committed last year to establishing a link. The UK carbon contract for December closed at a £64.81 per ton on Friday while benchmark EU allowances were at €86.55.    The price gap could shrink further over the next two years, as UK allowances move closer to EU permits, Moutaz Altaghlibi, Senior Energy Economist at ABN Amro wrote in a note on Nov. 5. That would mean UK firms having to pay more for permits. “Linking the systems should also improve liquidity, make carbon prices more consistent across Europe, and reduce CBAM-related costs and paperwork for trade between the UK and EU,” he said.  Although the idea of re-linking carbon markets has been discussed for years, Britain’s current Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also working to bring the UK closer to Europe on a broader level. A key parameter in the agreement will be the cap on emissions in the UK ETS. The EU is set to recognize emissions caps in the British system in the 2028-2030 period, according to people with knowledge of the issue. From 2031, the annual UK issuance will be capped at 7.1% of permits to be issued in the EU ETS.   The UK will also create its own Market Stability Reserve, a mechanism that the EU has had for more than a decade to automatically control the supply of carbon permits and alleviate a glut of allowances that emerged and weighed on prices. It will start with at least 29.5 million allowances when the deal enters into force.  Before the start of 2030, a decision will be taken on adjustments to ensure that the amount of permits in the UK MSR corresponds to at least 6.7% of allowances in the EU ETS reserve in 2029.   As part of the draft deal, negotiators have also agreed to keep rules aligned over time, with Britain obliged to integrate European rules into its law.  The deal will need to be ratified by both the UK and the EU, in a procedure that involves the European Parliament and member states in the EU Council. It will enter into force a month after the last notification regarding the two other deliverables of the upcoming summit: an SPS agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary standards and a solution on a youth mobility scheme, known as YES.  The parties may also choose to apply the deal on a provisional basis before its entry into force.

item.title: Coca-Cola's India bottling arm HCCH files DRHP for 997.5 million-share IPO
item.description: The proposed IPO will be entirely an offer for sale by promoter Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings, with no proceeds going to HCCH; the company reported ₹11,663 crore in FY26 revenue ...
item.dc:creator: Sharleen Dsouza
item.content:encoded: Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings Limited (HCCH), the holding company of Coca-Cola's Indian bottling business, has established a dominant position in the Southern and Western parts of the country through a multi-year re-franchising process. “Our business and operations have undergone changes as a result of a multi-year re-franchising process. Between financial years 2024 and 2026, we sold our business undertakings in Rajasthan, Bihar, Jharkhand, Northeast India, parts of West Bengal and North Gujarat (collectively, the “Refranchised Units”) to other TCCC Bottlers by way of slump sales,” the firm said in its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) filed on Saturday.  It has the licence to prepare, package, distribute, and sell The Coca-Cola Company’s (TCCC) beverages exclusively in 10 states and four union territories, keeping its operations concentrated in the South and West.  HCCH can sell in all of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep. It faces restrictions in Diu, parts of Puducherry and Karaikal and Mahe.  In areas where it operates, the bottler had a network of 2,273 distributors as of June 30, 2026 and over half of them have been with the company for over five years.  Its production footprint comprises 14 owned production facilities with an aggregate installed capacity of 1,291.1 million unit cases per annum, supported by eight co-pack units. “Collectively, these facilities operated 90 bottling lines, including 77 owned bottling lines and 13 bottling lines at co-pack units, and were complemented by a network of 23 warehouses,” it said.  India was one of the five largest markets for the Coca-Cola System by unit case volume for calendar year 2025, the DRHP stated.  “Our recent strategic reorientation encompassing completion of the re-franchising process, addition of Jubilant Beverages as one of our promoters, leadership and organisational enhancements, and renewed focus on execution, has, we believe, established our foundation for future growth,” HCCH said.  The proposed initial public offering (IPO) comprises an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 997.5 million equity shares with a face value of ₹10 by promoter Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings Pte. Ltd. The entire proceeds from the offer will go to the promoter selling shares. Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages, the primary bottling unit of HCCH, is one of Coca-Cola's largest bottling partners in India. Coca-Cola's decision to dilute its stake in its Indian bottling business is part of a larger global strategy to move away from bottling operations and adopt an asset-light, franchise-led business model. Its portfolio of brands includes Coca-Cola, Thums Up, Sprite, Fanta, Limca, Monster, Schweppes, Kinley, Maaza and Minute Maid. Currently, Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings Pte. Ltd. holds 60 per cent of HCCH's equity share capital, while Jubilant Beverages Limited holds the remaining 40 per cent. Jubilant Beverages became one of the promoters of HCCH in July 2025. The book-running lead managers for the IPO are Kotak Investment Banking, Citi Global Markets India, J.P. Morgan India, Morgan Stanley India, Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs India and IIFL Capital Services. HCCH's profit attributable to shareholders stood at ₹408.45 crore in the April-June quarter, compared to ₹1,054.4 crore in the year ago period. Its revenue from operations rose 17 per cent to ₹4,310.17 crore during the period. In FY26, its revenue from operations stood at ₹11,663.24 crore, compared to ₹12,869.54 crore in FY25, down 9 per cent. The company was the largest non-alcoholic ready-to-drink beverage company by revenue operating exclusively in India in FY26, the DRHP said citing a report by The Knowledge Company (TKC). It stated that it has the highest market share of 37.2 per cent in the overall soft drinks and packaged drinking water category. In the still category, which includes its brands Maaza and Minute Maid, it has a market share of 42.6 per cent. It has a market share of 12.9 per cent in the energy drinks segment and 9.7 per cent in the packaged drinking water segment.
